title: Best Air Filters for Allergies: How to Choose
h1: What Are the Best HVAC Air Filters for Allergies?
description: The best air filter for allergies is the highest MERV rating your system handles well, often MERV 11 to 13. Learn how to pick one and when to change it.
quick_answer: For most homes, a pleated filter rated MERV 11 to 13 is the best choice for allergies. It catches pollen, dust mite debris, pet dander and many mold spores without choking airflow in most systems. Make sure it fits snugly, change it on time, and run the fan enough to pass air through it. True HEPA usually needs a separate unit.
body:
What do MERV ratings mean?

MERV is a standard scale from 1 to 16 that rates how well a filter catches particles of different sizes. Higher numbers catch smaller particles. For allergy sufferers, the useful range is roughly:

  • MERV 1 to 4: Thin fiberglass filters. They protect the equipment from large debris but do very little for allergies.
  • MERV 8: A basic pleated filter. Catches pollen and larger dust, a solid step up.
  • MERV 11: Catches finer dust, pet dander and more mold spores. A good allergy filter for most homes.
  • MERV 13: Catches even smaller particles, including much of the fine smoke particulate from wildfires. Great if your system can handle it.

Some stores use their own rating names instead of MERV. If you can, look for the MERV number on the box so you can compare apples to apples.

Can a higher-rated filter hurt my system?

It can if the system isn't built for it. A denser filter has more resistance, and a system with a small return or a single undersized filter slot may struggle to pull enough air through. Signs of trouble include weak airflow at the vents, a whistling return grille, a coil that freezes up in summer, or a furnace that shuts off on high temperature.

A deeper filter is the usual fix. A 4 or 5 inch media filter in a proper cabinet has far more surface area than a 1 inch filter, so it can filter finely without restricting airflow as much. It also lasts longer between changes.

What about HEPA, electrostatic and washable filters?

HEPA filters are excellent, but they're too restrictive for most residential HVAC systems to use in the main filter slot. In a home, HEPA usually means a portable purifier in the bedroom or a dedicated bypass unit installed on the system.

Washable electrostatic filters can be convenient, but they tend to filter less than a good pleated filter and lose effectiveness if they aren't cleaned and fully dried on schedule. A damp filter going back into the system is a mold risk.

Electronic air cleaners and ionizers vary widely. Avoid anything that produces ozone, which irritates the lungs.

How often should you change an allergy filter?

There's no single answer, but here's a practical starting point for 1 inch pleated filters: check monthly and change every one to three months. Change sooner if you have pets, you're doing remodeling work, or there's wildfire smoke in the area. Deeper media filters typically last several months, depending on the manufacturer and your home.

Write the date on the filter frame when you put it in. It's the easiest way to stay on schedule.

A quick visual check works too. Hold the used filter up to a light. If you can barely see light through it, or the pleats are coated gray, it's done. Don't try to vacuum and reuse a disposable pleated filter. It damages the media and doesn't restore its performance.

What else helps allergies besides the filter?

A filter only cleans the air that passes through it. A few other things make a real difference:

  1. Seal the filter slot. Gaps around the filter let unfiltered air sneak past it. A filter that's even slightly too small isn't doing its job.
  2. Run the fan. In mild coastal weather the system may not run much, so the filter isn't working either. Some thermostats have a circulate mode that runs the fan part of each hour.
  3. Seal leaky return ducts. Returns in the attic or garage that leak pull in dust and insulation fibers before the air ever reaches the filter.
  4. Close windows on high-pollen and Santa Ana days. Those dry, gusty winds kick up a lot of dust and pollen.
  5. Add a bedroom purifier. A portable HEPA unit in the room where you sleep is one of the easiest wins for allergy sufferers.

If you're not sure what your system can handle, our indoor air quality technicians can check your return size, recommend a filter and install a media cabinet if it makes sense. Check current specials before you book.
faqs: Is MERV 13 too high for a home HVAC system?

Not for many systems, but it depends on your return ductwork and filter size. A MERV 13 filter in a deeper media cabinet usually works well. In a single undersized 1 inch slot it can restrict airflow. If you notice weaker airflow or new noises after switching, have a technician check it.
Do expensive filters really help with allergies?

Higher-rated pleated filters catch more of the fine particles that trigger allergies, so yes, they generally help more than cheap fiberglass ones. Price alone means little, though. Compare MERV ratings, make sure the filter fits snugly and change it on schedule.
Should I run my HVAC fan all the time for allergies?

Running the fan more often means more air passes through the filter, which helps. Running it nonstop uses more electricity and can raise humidity in summer by re-evaporating moisture from the coil. A circulate setting that runs the fan part of each hour is a good middle ground.
Where is the air filter in my house?

In most Southern California homes it is behind a return grille in a hallway ceiling or wall, or at the furnace itself in a hall closet, garage or attic. Some homes have more than one return, each with its own filter. Check them all.
